documents.title: The ADOIT Solution Guides
documents.summary: The ADOIT Solution Guides provide step-by-step instructions based on consulting experience to help users efficiently master key Enterprise Architecture initiatives like Application Portfolio Management and Capability-based Planning within ADOIT.
documents.content:
Thank you for your interest in our ADOIT solutions! We are excited to help you transform your Enterprise Architecture initiatives into actionable results.

To ensure you can seamlessly transition from strategy to execution, we have developed these dedicated Solution Guides. Based on our years of consulting experience, we have carefully selected these solutions to reflect industry best practices. They provide step-by-step instructions tailored to the scenarios featured on our website.

Our goal is simple: to empower you to master these key EA initiatives within ADOIT quickly and efficiently, ensuring you achieve your desired outcomes and demonstrate value to your stakeholders in record time.

Select the solution you are interested in to receive the relevant information:
• Application Portfolio Management
• Application Compliance Assessment
• Capability-based Planning
• Enterprise Architecture Design
• Scenario Planning
• Technology Lifecycle Management
• End-User Application Governance

note

If you are wondering where to start, our best practices have shown that the most effective path begins with establishing an Application Portfolio, followed by Capability-based Planning.

children.title: Solution Guide - Application Portfolio Management
children.summary: Introduction to the Application Portfolio Management solution in ADOIT, aimed at transforming Enterprise Architecture initiatives into actionable results.
children.content: Thank you for your interest in our ADOIT solutions! We are excited to help you transform your Enterprise Architecture initiatives into actionable results.

children.title: Before You Start
children.summary: This guide requires completion of the ADOIT Quick Start Guide before starting the Application Portfolio Management Solution Guide.
children.content: This guide assumes that you’ve already completed the ADOIT Quick Start Guide. If your ADOIT environment is already set up, you can start directly with the Application Portfolio Management Solution Guide.

children.title: Bring Clarity to Your Application Landscape
children.summary: Application Portfolio Management helps organizations bring clarity to their application landscape by evaluating applications in context of business value, technical health, and strategic relevance to support aligned investment decisions.
children.content:
Your organization probably has more applications than it wants and less clarity than it needs.

Some applications clearly support the business. Others slow things down, cost money, or simply stay around because no one touches them. Application Portfolio Management helps you bring order into this landscape and create a clear basis for decisions.

You don’t start by debating individual systems. You look at applications in context: business value, technical health, and strategic relevance. This makes it easier to agree on where to invest, what to modernize, and what to retire.

Application Portfolio Management creates a shared basis for business and IT and helps turn application discussions into aligned decisions.

children.title: Why Application Portfolio Management in ADOIT
children.summary: ADOIT supports Application Portfolio Management with an ArchiMate-based repository, powerful views, and guided workspaces to enable shared, consistent portfolio decisions and transition from transparency to action.
children.content:
Effective Application Portfolio Management requires more than lists and slides.

ADOIT combines an ArchiMate-based repository to map applications and their relationships with business processes, technologies, and data, powerful views to explore and understand the application landscape, and guided workspaces to assess investment strategies and define roadmaps together with business peers.

This gives you a shared and consistent foundation for portfolio decisions and helps you move from transparency to action.

children.title: How it Works in ADOIT
children.summary: Start Application Portfolio Management with a small prototype of representative Application Components to focus on outcomes like reports and visualizations before refining the setup and scaling.
children.content:
note

Important: Start with a flat list of a few representative Application Components and work in a small setup team. The initial goal is not to capture the full application landscape, but to build a working prototype together.

Use this prototype to walk through the entire APM process end to end. Focus on the results you want to achieve, especially reports, visualizations, and decision support.

Along the way, you will see which information is actually needed to support these outcomes. Only then refine your setup and structure accordingly before onboarding your colleagues. This keeps the approach lightweight, outcome-driven, and easy to adapt over time.

children.title: Choose the lean metamodel profile as a starting point
children.summary: Use the 'ADOIT for lean Architecture Fans' metamodel profile as a simple yet effective starting point for Application Portfolio Management, expanding it as needed based on actual requirements.
children.content:
As already recommended in the Quick Start Guide choose the 'ADOIT for lean Architecture Fans' metamodel profile. It is a proven and pragmatic starting point that keeps things simple while still allowing meaningful analysis.

It simplifies the complexity of ArchiMate while ensuring you have all the objects and relations needed to fully use our offered solutions and sample models.

From there you can expand step by step once you know which elements and relationships are actually needed for your Application Portfolio Management practice.

children.title: Establish a single source of truth
children.summary: Establish a minimal application inventory in ADOIT by creating Application Components, assigning owners, lifecycle states, and business units, focusing initially on a small prototype to build a foundation for further modeling.
children.content:
There is a lot of information you could capture in an application inventory, such as application owners, required system software, business units that use the application, supported business processes, and realized capabilities. We’ll get to that later. For now, focus on the bare minimum.

Steps:
1. Select a folder in the Object Explorer where you want to build your application inventory. In larger organizations you may use multiple folders to manage access rights. For now, stick to the structure you already defined in the Quick Start Guide.
1. Create a first list of applications. Start with three to five Application Components you know well. These will serve as your prototype and reference for all future applications.

note

In ADOIT applications are called Application Components following ArchiMate.

1. Assign an application owner to each Application Component. To do so, open the notebook of an Application Component, click on edit and fill in the relation attribute ‘Responsible business actors’ in the Chapter ‘Organisation’.

note

The initial user list was created in the Quick Start Guide. If you need additional users you can create them in the ADOIT Administration.

1. Set the lifecycle state. Switch to the chapter ‘Lifecycle’ and define the Lifecycle State for each application. Most likely your prototype applications are ‘In production’.
2. Capture the using Business Units. Document which business units use each application. Create the required business units using the element type ‘Business Actor’. Reuse the folder structure from your Quick-Start-Setup and create only what you need for your prototype applications.

I think you are getting the hang of it now. Let’s focus on the outcomes next especially the reports and visualizations. We will continue shaping the modeling guidelines later.

children.title: Visualize your application landscape
children.summary: Early visualization of the application landscape using saved queries and ADOIT Analyses helps understand needed information and communicate the portfolio effectively with visualizations like Box-in-Box diagrams.
children.content:
So far we have only captured a small amount of data. That is perfectly fine. Starting with visualizations early helps you understand which information you actually need.

Steps:
1. Create a simple list of all applications. The most basic report is a list of all Application Components. Create this list and share it with your colleagues. Go to ‘Find’ create the list of Application Components and click ‘Share’. Save it as a saved query with the name ‘Application Portfolio’.
1. A list is often not the best way to communicate an application landscape. Depending on what you want to show, a visual representation can provide a much better overview.

To create and manage such views, use ADOIT Analyses.

Go to Find -> Explorer -> Model Explorer and review the existing structure. Then create a folder named ‘Application Portfolio’. This is where you store your analysis.
2. Create your first analysis. Even with limited data you can already build useful visualizations. Create an analysis model, store it in the Application Portfolio folder and select the saved query ‘Application Portfolio’ as your data source.
3. Add a Box-in-Box visualization. Configure it as Business Actor to Application Component and use Lifecycle State as the color.

You now have your first visualization. From here you can explore additional visualization types as needed.

children.title: Review the Lean Architecture Profile and add more visualizations
children.summary: Extend the Lean Architecture Profile pragmatically to support additional visualizations such as matrices and timelines, using ADOIT Administration for adding elements or attributes and Groupings for lightweight classification.
children.content:
Now take a closer look at the Lean Architecture Profile and extend it just enough to support additional visualizations.

With a small number of additional elements and relationships you can already create most common views such as Matrices, Gantt style timelines and further portfolio views.

Stay pragmatic. Add visualizations only where you are confident you can collect the required data. Follow a minimum viable architecture approach. You can always expand later.

note

If something important is missing, you can add additional concepts. This can be done using the ADOIT Administration. There you find all ArchiMate elements that can be added.

Furthermore, you can add additional fields – so called Attributes – using the Property Management Component.

A lightweight way to add structure without changing the metamodel is to use Groupings. In ArchiMate, Groupings work like a simple tagging mechanism.

Create elements of type Grouping, give them meaningful names, for example to classify applications according to Gartner’s PACE-Layered Application Strategy such as System of Record, System of Differentiation, or System of Innovation, and assign them to your elements using the Aggregation relationship.

children.title: Keep Portfolio Data Current with Forms
children.summary: ADOIT Forms enables maintaining up-to-date portfolio data via surveys, allowing non-expert colleagues to contribute; customize and distribute the predefined 'Application Update' template to collect necessary information.
children.content:
At this point you might be wondering how to keep all this information up to date. ADOIT Forms is designed exactly for this purpose.

ADOIT Forms allows you to collect and maintain information through simple surveys. Your colleagues can contribute without needing to understand your detailed setup or ArchiMate.

In the Quick Start Guide, you already activated ADOIT Forms, including the predefined template ‘Application Update’. Review the template and check whether it covers all the information you want to keep up to date. Add questions if something is missing and remove questions if it feels too detailed.

Activate the template and distribute it. For the applications you already captured the assigned ‘Responsible Business Actors’ will receive an email request. In ADOIT Forms you can track the status and manage the templates.

children.title: You are ready to launch
children.summary: Before broad rollout, validate the portfolio structure, forms, and visualizations with a core team, then capture all applications, assign owners, import existing lists if available, and distribute update forms to keep data current.
children.content:
The structure is in place. Before rolling this out broadly, run a final dry run with your core setup team. Capture a few additional applications, assign application owners, and validate that the structure, forms, and visualizations work as expected.

Once you are confident, bring your application portfolio to life. Capture all remaining applications and assign the Responsible Business Actors or application owners. If you already have an application list in Excel, use the Excel import to save time. Then distribute the Application Update form to collect the data needed for your minimum viable architecture and keep the portfolio up to date.

children.title: Additional tips
children.summary: Additional tips include using Application Investment Planning and Application-based Roadmap workspaces for strategy and evolution, and consulting rights management documentation if write-access control is needed.
children.content:
➢ To define investment strategies for your applications, use the workspace Application Investment Planning.

➢ Based on those strategies, use the workspace Application-based Roadmap to further evolve and steer your portfolio.

➢ If too many teams or users have write-access to applications, take a look at the rights management documentation next. Don’t let this slow you down though. In many cases, getting first results matters more than perfect permissions.

children.title: Solution Guide - Application Compliance Assessment
children.summary: Introduction to the Application Compliance Assessment solution in ADOIT, aimed at transforming Enterprise Architecture initiatives into actionable results.
children.content: Thank you for your interest in our ADOIT solutions! We are excited to help you transform your Enterprise Architecture initiatives into actionable results.

children.title: Before You Start
children.summary: Before starting Application Compliance Assessment, ensure the ADOIT Quick Start Guide is completed and manually add missing object types and relations (Constraint and associations) to the 'ADOIT for lean Architecture Fans' metamodel profile as this solution is not fully supported out-of-the-box yet.
children.content:
This guide assumes that you've already completed the ADOIT Quick Start Guide. If your ADOIT environment is already set up, you can start directly with the Application Compliance Assessment Solution Guide.

Important Note on Metamodel Configuration:

Please be aware that this solution is currently not fully supported by the 'ADOIT for lean Architecture Fans' metamodel profile out-of-the-box:
• The object type Principle is already included in the profile.
• The object type Constraint is not included in the profile.
• The relations Application Component < Association < Principle and Application Component < Association < Constraint are not included in the profile.

To utilize this workflow today, you must first add the missing object type and relations manually to the profile via the ADOIT Administration.

However, this manual setup is only temporary: the entire solution will be natively included and available by default in the lean metamodel profile starting with our upcoming release.

children.title: Evaluate Application Components Against What Matters
children.summary: Application Compliance Assessment helps systematically evaluate Application Components against evolving compliance criteria and standards, making risks visible and actionable within ADOIT's repository and workspaces.
children.content:
Compliance is no longer a checkbox exercise. Regulations evolve, architecture standards multiply, and application landscapes grow faster than governance can keep up. Without a structured way to evaluate Application Components against the criteria that matter, risks stay hidden until audits, incidents, or transformation projects force reactive decisions.

The Application Compliance Assessment solution helps you systematically evaluate Application Components against critical compliance criteria. You identify risks early, understand exactly where action is required, and make compliance a meaningful input into portfolio and architecture decisions.

Whether you align to ISO 25010 quality characteristics, SABSA Business Attributes, or regulations such as the EU AI Act or DORA, ADOIT gives you a dedicated workspace to assign criteria, assess fulfillment, visualize gaps, and plan remediation.

Compliance becomes visible and actionable in your current repository state - not buried in spreadsheets.

children.title: Why Application Compliance Assessment in ADOIT
children.summary: ADOIT combines an ArchiMate repository with collaborative workspaces, dashboards, and roadmaps to enable living compliance assessments that integrate with portfolio governance and support business and IT stakeholders.
children.content:
Effective compliance assessment requires more than static policy documents. You need a living connection between your application inventory, the criteria you must meet, and the decisions that follow.

ADOIT combines an ArchiMate-based repository with guided workspaces for collaborative assessment, configurable dashboards for ongoing monitoring, and roadmap workspaces to turn findings into planned change. Business and IT stakeholders can contribute without deep modelling expertise, and assessment results are stored in the repository for reporting, audit preparation, and portfolio governance.

This gives you a shared foundation for compliance decisions and helps you move from identifying gaps to closing them.

children.title: How Compliance Calculation Works in ADOIT
children.summary: Compliance calculation in ADOIT uses either Principles or Constraints exclusively per workspace, stores assessments directly in the repository notebooks, and calculates compliance only from criteria assigned within each workspace.
children.content:
Before you start assessing Application Components, understand how ADOIT calculates compliance. These rules apply throughout this guide and shape how you set up workspaces and interpret results.
• Principles or Constraints - not both. Compliance can only be calculated using one criterion type at a time: either Principles or Constraints. When you create an Application Compliance Assessment workspace, you choose which type is active. The workspace then works exclusively with that type for assigning criteria, assessing fulfillment, and displaying summary views.
• Assessments are written directly to the repository. When you assess an Application Component in the workspace, the value is saved immediately in the repository, in the Notebook of the respective object. It works the other way round as well: if the assessment is changed directly in the Notebook or in another workspace, the workspace shows the changed value. In ADOIT 21 LTS, there is no separate assessment history - the workspace always displays the values currently stored in the repository.
• Only the criteria of the workspace count. You can create several workspaces that each cover a specific topic - for example one per standard, business unit, or framework. This helps you limit the assessment to the relevant Application Components and run collaborative reviews. The compliance values in a workspace are calculated only from the Principles or Constraints assigned within that workspace.

Keep these three points in mind when you read the sections below. They explain why workspace setup, repository content, and reassessment behaviour work the way they do in ADOIT.

children.title: How it Works in ADOIT
children.summary: Start Application Compliance Assessment with a small prototype of Application Components to walk through the full process collaboratively, focusing on outcomes before scaling; having an established Application Portfolio is recommended.
children.content:
Important: Start with a small set of representative Application Components and work in a focused setup team. The initial goal is not to assess your entire application landscape at once, but to build a working prototype together.

Use this prototype to walk through the full compliance assessment process end to end, from scoping Application Components and assigning criteria to assessing fulfillment, reviewing the compliance landscape through different visualizations, and planning remediation. Focus on the outcomes you want to achieve, especially heatmaps, dashboards, and decision support.

Along the way, you will see which tools, criteria and data are actually needed to support these outcomes. Only then refine your setup and scale to additional Application Components and frameworks. This keeps the approach lightweight, outcome-driven, and easy to adapt over time.

Best Practice:

To maximize the value of Application Compliance Assessment, we recommend having your Application Portfolio established first. At a minimum, a list of Application Components is required to scope, evaluate, and track compliance effectively.

You can find more information on Application Portfolio Management in ADOIT in our dedicated APM Solution Guide.

children.title: Choose the lean metamodel profile as a starting point
children.summary: Use the 'ADOIT for lean Architecture Fans' metamodel profile as a pragmatic starting point for Capability-based Planning to keep analysis simple yet meaningful.
children.content: As already recommended in the Quick Start Guide choose the 'ADOIT for lean Architecture Fans' metamodel profile. It is a proven and pragmatic starting point that keeps things simple while still allowing meaningful analysis.

children.title: Phase 1: Run the Application Compliance Assessment Workspace
children.summary: Create an Application Compliance Assessment workspace via the Workspaces scenario, configure members, privacy, and choose active compliance criteria type (Principles or Constraints) to start the collaborative assessment process.
children.content:
The Application Compliance Assessment workspace guides you through four collaborative steps: Scope, Compliance Criteria, Assessment, and Summary. Access it via the Workspaces scenario in the top-left scenario dropdown.

Create the workspace:
1. Open the Workspaces page → New workspace → select the Application Compliance Assessment template.
1. Complete the setup wizard: Name and description, add colleagues as members or admins, and configure privacy if needed. Then choose your compliance criteria Principles or Constraints - only one type is active per workspace. This choice determines how ADOIT calculates compliance for this assessment (see How Compliance Calculation Works in ADOIT above).
2. Click Create workspace to start.

children.title: Step 1: Scope
children.summary: In the Scope step, select Application Components to evaluate using filters and insights, starting with a small known set and expanding as the prototype matures.
children.content:
Select the Application Components you want to evaluate.

Steps:
1. Open your Application Compliance Assessment workspace and go to the Scope step.
2. In the left pane, browse available Application Components and click Add to include them in the assessment. Use Add all or Remove all for bulk actions.
3. Apply filters to narrow the list: other workspaces, groups, investment strategy (TIME), and lifecycle state. Combine multiple filter conditions as needed.
4. Open Insights on any element to review context before adding it to scope.
5. Start with three to five Application Components you know well. Expand once your prototype assessment produces useful results.

children.title: Step 2 - Compliance Criteria
children.summary: Assign compliance criteria (Principles or Constraints) to scoped Application Components, create new criteria if needed, and use filters to manage assignments; ISO 25010 criteria can be imported via a provided template.
children.content:
Assign compliance criteria to each scoped Application Component. Depending on your workspace setup, you work exclusively with Principles or Constraints - only one type is active per workspace.

Investment strategy and lifecycle state are shown per component to help you prioritise which Application Components need which criteria.

Steps:
1. Go to the Compliance Criteria step.
2. Select an Application Component and click Assign Principle or Assign Constraint (the label depends on your workspace setup).
3. Search and select an existing criterion from the repository, or type a new name and press Enter to create one directly in the workspace.
4. Click Show more to open tabs for criteria already assigned to the component and for all existing criteria in the repository.
5. Expand a criterion to view or edit its Description if needed.
6. Use filters to search Application Components by investment strategy or lifecycle state, and to filter criteria by Application Component.

note

ISO 25010 bonus: To assess Application Components against ISO 25010 quality characteristics without manual data entry, use the downloadable import file provided with this solution. It lets you import all ISO 25010 criteria as ArchiMate constraints in one step. You can download our ISO 25010 template here.

Set up your workspace for constraints before importing.

children.title: Step 3 - Assessment
children.summary: Assess fulfillment of each assigned compliance criterion per Application Component using a standardized five-point scale, leveraging Insights and inviting colleagues to contribute without modeling expertise.
children.content:
Assess how well each Application Component fulfills each assigned criterion. The evaluation is performed strictly per Application Component and per assigned criterion.

Steps:
1. Go to the Assessment step.
2. For each combination of Application Component and assigned criterion, select a fulfillment score on the standardized five-point scale:• 1 - Fully met
• 2 - Mostly met
• 3 - Partially met
• 4 - Weakly met
• 5 - Not met
3. Use Insights per element to review supporting information while you assess.
4. Invite colleagues to contribute. Workspace members can capture assessments without ArchiMate modelling expertise.

children.title: Step 4 - Summary
children.summary: Review compliance results in the Summary step with KPIs, fulfillment charts, heatmaps, and tables to identify critical gaps and prioritize actions based on workspace-specific assigned criteria.
children.content:
Review a complete overview of your Application Components and their compliance posture. The Summary step aggregates results into KPIs and interactive views - including a fulfillment status chart, a dynamic heatmap, and table views per Application Component and per criterion - so you can spot critical gaps and decide where action is needed. Remember that these values are calculated only from the Principles or Constraints assigned within this workspace.

Steps:
1. Go to the Summary step after assessments are complete.
2. Review the KPI counts and open the Fulfillment status pie chart via Show chart.
3. Explore the Heatmap to spot critical gaps - combinations where Application Components score poorly against specific criteria.
4. Switch between the per Application and per Guideline table views to analyse results from different perspectives.
5. Use these findings to decide which Application Components need immediate attention and which criteria drive the most risk.

children.title: Phase 2: Build a Compliance Dashboard
children.summary: Build a Configurable Dashboard in the Design & Document scenario to monitor compliance with widgets showing controls and Application Components metrics, reducing manual reporting effort.
children.content:
After completing the workspace assessment, monitor compliance using Configurable Dashboards. Dashboards aggregate current repository data into a personalised, widget-based layout that colleagues can open, share, and refresh without modelling access.

Centralised criteria tracking and automated dashboard views can reduce the manual effort spent on compliance reporting and audit preparation by up to 50% - aligned with standard IT-GRC analyst benchmarks.

Steps:
1. Switch to the Design & Document scenario via the top-left scenario dropdown.
2. Open the Dashboards page → Create Dashboard → enter a name (for example "Application Compliance Overview") → Create.
3. Click + Add widget and drag widgets from the widget library onto your dashboard.
4. Configure each widget, reposition and resize as needed, then Save.

We recommend the following widgets to build a comprehensive compliance dashboard - grouped by controls and Application Components.

Controls:
• Number widget - Read the total number of controls at a glance
• Table widget - List all active controls (principles or constraints)
• Pie chart widget - Show which type of controls you have - for example whether they belong to ISO 25010, SABSA, or another framework

Application Components:
• Number widget - See the total number of Application Components in scope
• Table widget - Display all evaluated Application Components
• Bar chart widget - Visualise the average fulfillment score across Application Components

children.title: Phase 3: Plan Remediation with the Application-Based Roadmap
children.summary: Use the Application-Based Roadmap workspace to plan, prioritize, schedule, and track remediation actions addressing compliance gaps collaboratively with stakeholders, turning assessment findings into planned change.
children.content:
Assessment findings only create value when they lead to action. Use the Application-Based Roadmap workspace to plan and schedule the changes required to close compliance gaps.

Actively mitigating critical gaps can drive a 10% to 20% reduction in non-compliant or redundant Application Components over time - aligned with standard APM industry benchmarks.

Steps:
1. Open the Workspaces scenario → New workspace → select the Application-Based Roadmap template.
2. Complete the setup wizard. Choose your prioritisation method (Value vs. Effort or Eisenhower Matrix) and define time periods (months, quarters, or years).
3. In Scope, add the Application Components that surfaced as non-compliant or partially compliant in your assessment.
4. In Requirements, capture the changes needed to improve fulfillment - for example architecture changes, technology updates, or process adjustments tied to specific criteria.
5. In Priority, assess each requirement and rank what to address first.
6. In Schedule, assign requirements to time periods so remediation is planned, not reactive.
7. In Status, track progress as changes are implemented.
8. Review the Summary to communicate the roadmap to business and IT stakeholders.

note

Workspaces are designed for collaboration. Invite application owners and business peers so remediation plans reflect both compliance requirements and operational reality. Assessment results are stored in the repository and can be referenced in analyses, colouring, and Insights views.

children.title: ArchiMate Elements and Relations for this Solution
children.summary: Key ArchiMate elements for Application Compliance Assessment include Application Component, Principle, and Constraint (the latter requiring manual addition to the metamodel profile).
children.content:
If you use the 'ADOIT for Lean Architecture Fans' metamodel profile as recommended earlier in this guide, the following elements are central to this solution:
• Application Component - Application Components evaluated for compliance
• Principle - Compliance criterion
• Constraint - Compliance criterion (must currently be added to the profile manually)

children.title: Solution Guide - Capability-based Planning
children.summary: Introduction to the Capability-based Planning solution in ADOIT, aimed at transforming Enterprise Architecture initiatives into actionable results.
children.content: Thank you for your interest in our ADOIT solutions! We are excited to help you transform your Enterprise Architecture initiatives into actionable results.

children.title: Before You Start
children.summary: This guide assumes completion of the ADOIT Quick Start Guide before starting the Capability-based Planning Solution Guide.
children.content: This guide assumes that you’ve already completed the ADOIT Quick Start Guide. If your ADOIT environment is already set up, you can start directly with the Capability-based Planning Solution Guide.

children.title: Plan Investments Where They Matter Most
children.summary: Capability-based Planning focuses on aligning investments with strategic business capabilities, providing a shared, business-friendly view that connects strategy, architecture, and execution for aligned decision-making.
children.content:
Capability-based Planning helps you focus on what your organization really needs to be good at. Capabilities give you a simple, business-friendly view that connects strategy, architecture, and execution without getting lost in details.

You don’t start with systems or technologies. You start with the Capabilities that matter for your strategy. You look at where they stand today, where they need to improve, and where investment will create real value.

Capability-based Planning creates a shared planning foundation for business and IT. Capabilities act as a common language that makes priorities visible, discussions easier, and decisions more aligned.

children.title: Why Capability-based Planning Matters in ADOIT
children.summary: ADOIT workspaces facilitate collaborative Capability-based Planning by guiding teams step-by-step, enabling business and IT experts to contribute without modeling expertise, resulting in aligned priorities and actionable plans.
children.content:
Capability-based Planning works best when business and IT plan together. It’s about collaboration, not complexity.

ADOIT workspaces are designed to support exactly this. They guide teams through planning step by step and make it easy for everyone to contribute. Business experts bring context, IT adds architectural insight, and no one needs to be a modeling expert to participate.

The result is a lightweight, collaborative planning approach that helps teams agree on priorities, steer investments, and turn strategy into action without turning it into an IT-only project.

children.title: Choose the lean metamodel profile as a starting point
children.summary: Start Capability-based Planning with the 'ADOIT for lean Architecture Fans' metamodel profile to simplify ArchiMate complexity while supporting meaningful analysis and expand as needed.
children.content:
As already recommended in the Quick Start Guide choose the 'ADOIT for lean Architecture Fans' metamodel profile. It is a proven and pragmatic starting point that keeps things simple while still allowing meaningful analysis.

It simplifies the complexity of ArchiMate while ensuring you have all the objects and relations needed to fully use our offered solutions and sample models.

From there you can expand step by step once you know which elements and relationships are actually needed for your Capability-based Planning practice.

children.title: Map what drives your business
children.summary: Create a Capability Map using Architecture Diagrams and Capability elements to visualize how the organization creates value, involving workshops to refine capabilities and optionally leveraging existing value streams or generic maps.
children.content:
Visualize how your organization creates value – from customer request to delivery. Give everyone a shared view of your core capabilities and where they contribute most.

In this step we create the capability map. It consists of a model of type ‘Architecture Diagram’ and objects of type ‘Capabilities’. For nice look and feel you can pimp it with graphics as we did.

note

If you have already defined a value stream or created a corresponding model, you can use it right away in the following steps.

Steps:
1. Open the Objects Explorer. Choose / create a folder where you want to store your Capabilities.
2. Open the Model Explorer. Choose / create a folder where you want to store your Capability Map model and create a ‘Architecture Diagram’ via the ‘New’ tab in the toolbar. Give your new Capability Map model a name.
3. Open your Capability Map model and start placing Value Streams and Capabilities on the modeling canvas.
4. Plan for about 50–100 Capabilities in total (that’s typical for many organizations).
5. Run short workshops with your colleagues to collect and refine your Capabilities together.
6. Use generic Capability Maps as inspiration if you like - but the best results come from building a map that fits your organization.

note

If you want a quick walkthrough, check out our online training.

For ArchiMate experts…

children.title: Reveal what powers each capability
children.summary: Link Capabilities to supporting systems, processes, and people to understand dependencies and impact, with insights growing as more elements like Application Components or Processes are connected.
children.content:
See how each capability is supported by systems, processes, and people. Understand dependencies and uncover where change will have the biggest impact.

For now, there’s not much to see here.

The insights will automatically grow once you start linking other Elements, such as Application Components or Processes, to your Capabilities.

At this stage, it’s enough to know that this information will become more valuable as your architecture evolves.

children.title: Pinpoint what needs improvement
children.summary: Use the object's notebook under 'Classification' to evaluate capabilities' performance, business fit, and strategic relevance, employing heatmaps and Capability Maps for clear communication and shared planning.
children.content:
Evaluate each capability’s performance, business fit, and strategic relevance in the object's notebook under the chapter 'Classification'. Use heatmaps to quickly identify strengths, weaknesses, and high-priority areas.

Communicate the results clearly. The best way to do this is by using your Capability Map. The more often you use it, the more familiar it becomes to your peers.

Over time, the Capability Map turns into a shared language. Your colleagues will start to trust it, use it, and rely on it as the joint planning basis for roadmap and investment decisions.

Steps:
1. Open Scenario Workspaces.
2. Create a Capability Investment Planning workspace.
3. Invite colleagues to join.

children.title: Design How Strategy Gets Executed
children.summary: Enterprise Architecture Design focuses on modeling Target Operating Models to make strategy execution explicit by connecting capabilities with people, processes, applications, and governance using ADOIT.
children.content:
Enterprise Architecture Design is about shaping how an organization actually works so strategy gets executed. In practice, this means designing (Target) Operating Models that describe how capabilities are brought to life through people, processes, applications, and governance.

Operating models are the architecture of execution. They define how decisions are made, how work flows, and how value is created day to day. The challenge is making the operating model explicit and turning it into something that can be discussed, designed, and evolved deliberately instead of remaining implicit and fragmented across documents and tools.

This is exactly where ADOIT comes in. With ADOIT, operating models become visible and tangible. You can model today’s setup, design target operating models, and connect them directly to strategy, capabilities, and execution-relevant elements. Instead of debating abstract concepts, you work with concrete architectural structures.

children.title: Why Enterprise Architecture Design in ADOIT
children.summary: Architecture Design in ADOIT reveals improvement opportunities, makes dependencies explicit, and promotes reuse for better prioritization and coordinated execution.
children.content:
Architecture Design helps you move from abstract strategy to concrete, executable structures by making operating models visible and actionable.
• Clear improvement opportunities

By breaking capabilities down into their internal structure, you can clearly see where things don’t work as intended. This helps you identify weak spots and derive well-founded strategic requirements that form a solid foundation for effective strategic planning.
• Visible dependencies and impact

Modeling capabilities in ArchiMate makes dependencies and mutual influences between processes, applications, data, and roles explicit. You can see how changes propagate, understand their impact, and use this insight to strengthen business cases and plan changes with greater confidence.
• Reuse and better execution decisions

By reusing architectural elements across capabilities, you make shared resources transparent and avoid redundancy. This supports better prioritization, more informed decisions, and coordinated execution across the organization.

children.title: Understand what powers your business
children.summary: Develop operating models per capability linking processes, systems, and people, focusing on relevant detail, ownership, reuse of architectural elements, and consistent modeling practices.
children.content:
Drill down into any capability to see the processes, systems, and people behind it. Reveal what drives or hinders performance and focus on what really moves the needle.

note

Start small. Begin by creating operating models for two to three Capabilities. Use this first iteration to learn what really matters and to define a common structure for all operating model diagrams, for example consistent swimlanes and a consistent set of element types.

Be mindful of the level of detail. Avoid overloading the models with too much detail and focus on what is relevant for understanding and decision-making. Keep in mind that these models need to stay up to date over time.

From the start, think about ownership. Each operating model should be easy to hand over to a Capability Owner, Domain Architect, or a similar role who can maintain and evolve it going forward.

Steps:
1. Create one operating model per Capability.

Start by creating one Architecture model for each Capability. In the Model Explorer, use a single folder called ‘Operating Models’ for your first iteration. Keeping everything in one place helps you move fast and keeps things simple. You can refine the folder structure later, for example to support rights management or reflect your organizational setup.
2. Prepare where architectural elements are stored

Operating models typically include business processes, roles, data objects, applications, and sometimes technology elements. Use the object folder structure predefined in the Quick Start Guide as a starting point. This gives you a clean and consistent setup without overthinking it upfront.
3. Create the Architecture Design model

Create a new model of type ‘Architecture Diagram’. This model represents the operating model for a single Capability.
4. Link the model to its Capability

Open the notebook of the Capability and assign the Architecture Diagram you just created. This ensures a clear and explicit connection between the Capability and its operating model.
5. Structure the model with swimlanes

Add swimlanes to structure your model. A proven starting point is the classic BADT structure: Business, Application, Data, Technology. This keeps the model readable and helps stakeholders orient themselves quickly.
6. Add and reuse architectural elements

Use objects that you have already created in other EA initiatives or solutions (such as Application Portfolio Management). It is essential to avoid creating duplicates within your repository at all costs. Add processes, data objects, application components, and other relevant elements to describe how the Capability works. Focus on consistency and reuse. Many elements used in one Capability will also be relevant for others.

note

Tips and Tricks for graphical modelling:
• Objects created directly in diagrams are automatically stored in the Object Explorer under personal > [your name] . Make sure to move them to the appropriate folder in your structure. Avoid leaving objects in the personal folder.
• Objects can be reused across multiple diagrams. Deleting an object from a diagram only removes it from that diagram. The object itself remains in the Object Explorer.
• Use SHIFT + DELETE if you want to remove an object completely from the repository, not just from a diagram.
• Before creating a new object, check whether it already exists. If duplicates occur, you can use Merge objects. Be aware that outgoing relationships are merged, while incoming relationships are kept only for the remaining object.

note

If you already use ADOIT for Application Portfolio Management or Capability-based Planning, reuse existing elements instead of creating new ones. This strengthens consistency across your architecture and increases the value of all related analyses.

children.title: Design and Compare Future Architectures With Confidence
children.summary: Scenario Planning in ADOIT enables designing, comparing, and evaluating future architectures via multiple scenarios without altering the baseline, facilitating informed decisions.
children.content:
With Scenario Planning in ADOIT, you can design, compare, and evaluate future architectures without touching your current baseline. Create alternative scenarios, explore their impact, and make informed decisions based on a clear and shared view of the architecture.

Scenario Planning helps you work through complex architecture decisions step by step. Instead of committing too early, you create and compare multiple future options and see how they differ in terms of cost, risk, dependencies, and long-term impact.

In ADOIT, each option is modeled as its own scenario. This gives business and IT a common language to discuss alternatives, understand trade-offs, and agree on the best way forward.

children.title: Why Scenario Planning Matters in ADOIT
children.summary: Scenario Planning provides a safe space to explore alternatives by reusing or adding elements without impacting the baseline, supporting trade-off analysis and consensus.
children.content:
ADOIT provides a central, trusted view of your architecture. Scenario Planning adds a dedicated space to think ahead without putting that baseline at risk.

You can reuse existing Elements, add new ones, or plan decommissioning while keeping the agreed architecture unchanged. This makes it easy to compare alternatives, discuss trade-offs, and agree on the best direction before anything is released into the curated repository.

children.title: Typical Scenario Planning Use Cases
children.summary: Common Scenario Planning use cases include sourcing decisions, modernization, consolidation, deployment models, data architecture variants, and integration strategies.
children.content:
• Build, Buy, or Combine: compare different sourcing options for delivering a new solution.
• Modernize or Replace: decide whether existing applications should be improved, replaced, or retired.
• Reuse, Consolidate, or Introduce: explore options to reduce redundancy and simplify the application landscape.
• On-Premise, Cloud, or Hybrid: evaluate different deployment models and their business impact.
• Data Architecture Variants: compare alternative approaches to managing and using data.
• Integration and API Strategies: Choose the most suitable way to connect systems and services.

children.content:

Steps:
1. Open the chosen scenario diagram and perform model validation. Correct all findings.
2. After the final decision, start creating new objects and relationships, and delete existing elements that are no longer relevant, as the implementation progresses.

note

This step is intentionally done manually. It gives you the flexibility to enrich the architecture with the right level of detail and to take action on required deviations during implementation, without overloading the Scenario with unnecessary information.

children.title: Manage Your IT Landscape with Confidence
children.summary: Technology Lifecycle Management helps proactively manage IT risks by tracking technology lifecycles, dependencies, and ownership to maintain a modern, secure IT landscape.
children.content:
Technology moves fast. What is standard today might be unsupported and risky tomorrow. Outdated technologies increase technical debt, cause unnecessary costs, and slow down your ability to innovate. Technology Lifecycle Management helps you bring transparency to your stack and manage risks proactively before they become urgent.

It is not just about keeping lists of software and servers. It is about understanding which critical applications rely on which technologies. By tracking end-of-life dates and establishing clear ownership, you build a solid foundation to retire legacy systems on time and keep your IT landscape modern, secure, and future-ready.

children.title: Why Technology Lifecycle Management in ADOIT
children.summary: ADOIT integrates technology management with business architecture, enabling impact analysis, AI-supported lifecycle data, and strategic decision-making.
children.content:
Effective technology management requires more than isolated spreadsheets. ADOIT connects your technology landscape directly to your business architecture. You can instantly see the impact of an expiring database version on your applications and business processes. With features like AI-supported lookup for lifecycle data and integrated roadmaps, you turn simple administration into strategic foresight.

This empowers you to uncover hidden risks, coordinate updates together with application owners, and make smarter investment decisions based on reliable data.

children.title: How it Works in ADOIT

children.content:
Bring structure to your IT landscape by defining a scalable reference model. By organizing technologies into logical domains and assigning clear ownership, you create a solid foundation for smarter architectural decisions. This results in a highly organized tech landscape where every technology has a clear place and purpose.

Steps:
1. Create the folder structure. Open the Object Explorer and create a new folder named “Technology Domains”.
2. Define your domains. We recommend defining technology domains on two levels to maintain a clean overview (e.g., Level 1: "Data Storage", Level 2: "Relational Database Systems").
3. Create folders for each high-level technology domain.
4. Create the technology domains. Use the element type “Grouping” to represent them. This allows you to cluster specific technologies later.

children.title: Get full visibility across IT

children.content:
The real value of technology management lies in understanding dependencies. Connect applications with the technologies they rely on to visualize and understand dependencies. This step improves data accuracy, uncovers hidden risks, and provides accurate technology mapping across your entire architecture.

Steps:
1. Collect your technologies. Within your domain folders, collect all technologies on level of major version. Use elements of type “System Software” to define the technology products in use.

note

Keep it lean: Define technologies only on the level of the Major Version (e.g., "Oracle 19c"). Do not go deeper (e.g., patches or minor builds). Detailed versioning is typically irrelevant for strategic EA activities and causes unnecessary maintenance work.

1. Fill in the essentials. For each System Software element, fill-in at minimum:• Name: Include the Major Version.
• Responsible Person: Who manages this technology?
• Application Components that use this System Software via Relation “System Software -> serves -> Application Component”.
• Add incoming relations “aggregates” from Grouping that represents the lowest level of technology domain.

children.title: Stay ahead of end-of-life
children.summary: Use AI-supported ‘End-of-Life Lookup’ to track technology lifecycles, create analyses with Box-in-Box visualizations, and apply color coding to monitor expiry dates proactively.
children.content:
Don't let expiration dates surprise you. Track lifecycles using ADOIT’s intelligent features to achieve Technology Lifecycle Control. By using AI-supported lookups, you can track expiry dates, plan replacements before they become urgent, ensuring proactive risk mitigation and reducing downtime.

Steps:
1. Enrich with AI. Use the AI-based ‘End-of-Life Lookup’ in the notebook of an object. It will not only find defined EOL dates from online sources but also provide a prognosis on upcoming EOL dates based on historical data patterns.
2. Create an analysis to track expiry dates via colour coding:
• Create a search that retrieves your first level groupings (Domains) restricted to the relevant folders.
• From your search results, create a Box-in-Box visualization to show when technologies will reach their end-of-life.
• For the Box-in-Box visualization use the following hierarchy: First level Groupings (Domains) → Groupings (Sub-domains) → System Software.
• Use colour coding to visualize expiry dates.

children.title: See what’s at risk
children.summary: Identify applications at risk from expiring technologies by visualizing expiry dates via color-coded analyses grouped by application components or capabilities.
children.content:
Understanding the technology is one thing; understanding the business impact is another. Identify which applications depend on expiring technologies to ensure Service Continuity. This view prioritizes updates and creates necessary Application Risk Awareness among stakeholders.

Steps:
1. Create an analysis to visualize the expiry dates via colour coding from the perspective of your application components:

- [Create a search](https://docs.boc-group.com/adoit/en/docs/user_manual/searc-000000/#searc-E00000) that retrieves your application components restricted to the relevant folders.- From your search results, create a [Box-in-Box visualization](https://docs.boc-group.com/adoit/en/docs/user_manual/modwv-00000/#modwv-01500) to show which technologies will reach their end-of-life that serve your application components.- For the [Box-in-Box visualization](https://docs.boc-group.com/adoit/en/docs/user_manual/modwv-00000/#modwv-01500) use the following hierarchy: Application Component → served by → System Software.- Use colour coding to visualize expiry dates.
2. Alternatively, you can also visualize the applications and underlying system softwares grouped by capabilities: Capability → realized by → Application Component → served by → System Software.

children.title: Keep the data updated

children.content:

Steps:

2. Review regularly. Use the predefined form “Technology: Data Update” to ask technology owners to review and update versions and lifecycle dates on a regular basis.
3. Know what's in use. Use the predefined form “Application: Data Update” (as mentioned in the Application Portfolio Management solution guide) and ensure the section for selecting the underlying Technologies is active. This lets Application Owners document their own dependencies.

children.title: Before You Start

children.title: Empower Innovation with Secure End-User Computing
children.summary: End-User Application Governance manages user-developed EUC applications by balancing innovation benefits with risks, ensuring visibility, compliance, and business continuity.
children.content:
In many companies, employees develop their own End User Computing (EUC) applications (such as Excel sheets, Access databases, or macros) to solve daily operational tasks. This grassroots innovation is highly beneficial, as it empowers teams, enhances flexibility, and significantly boosts productivity by reducing dependence on the IT department. In fact, a majority of organizations recognize that EUC applications improve overall productivity.

However, because these user-built tools often operate outside of IT's direct assessment, they naturally come with certain risks. Without proper awareness, organizations can face data integrity issues, a lack of documentation, and compliance challenges. For instance, about one-third of successful cyber-attacks target data stored in unmonitored infrastructure.

To stay resilient and scale innovation safely, companies need to bring visibility to these solutions. End-User Application Governance helps you manage these applications with well-informed, transparent, and compliant decisions across the enterprise. This approach allows you to fully embrace the advantages of EUC while actively reducing risks, safeguarding business continuity, and ensuring compliance with regulations like DORA and NIS2.

children.title: Why End-User Application Governance in ADOIT
children.summary: ADOIT enables proactive End-User Computing (EUC) governance by providing unified visibility, policy enforcement, change tracking, and audit trails to manage risks and ensure regulatory compliance while supporting innovation.
children.content:
Effectively managing EUC requires a proactive approach that combines policy enforcement, technology, and transparency without stifling innovation.

ADOIT provides a unified view of all applications and processes, including those created and maintained by end users. With ADOIT, you gain the visibility and governance needed to turn hidden risks into well-managed assets. It empowers you to establish governance policies, track changes, monitor audit trails, and ensure that all applications meet the required regulatory standards - giving both business and IT the confidence to innovate safely.

children.title: Make it easy for teams to register their tools
